name: Dexpanthenol

lead: Dexpanthenol (panthenol, provitamin B5) is a common moisturizer and ointment ingredient used to keep dry or irritated skin hydrated and calm, so it looks smoother and less flaky. It appears in barrier-supporting skincare, often at a few percent.

It is converted to pantothenic acid, part of coenzyme A that supports normal epithelial function, and acts as a humectant that draws water into the skin. It penetrates well and reaches high local concentrations. Research, including a 70th-anniversary review and a 2020 wound-healing review, has centred on wound healing, skin irritation and radiation-related skin reactions, mostly in small trials.

paras: People use it in creams, lotions and ointments applied to dry, chapped or irritated areas, often as part of a barrier-repair routine. Hydration shows up soon after application, while repair of irritated skin takes days.
Topical use is described as well tolerated in the reviews listed. This entry does not cover injected B-vitamin products.

angle.text: Dexpanthenol draws moisture into skin and supports the barrier, so dry, irritated skin looks smoother and calmer. It is a vitamin B5 derivative studied mainly for wound healing and skin irritation.

lead: Dexpanthenol (also panthenol, provitamin B5) is the stable alcohol analog of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). It is a common ingredient in moisturizers, ointments, lip care, shampoos and eye gels. People use it to keep skin soft, hydrated and calm, which supports a smoother-looking, less irritated complexion, and to help minor skin damage heal with less visible marking.[1][2] It penetrates skin well and reaches high local concentrations when applied in a suitable vehicle such as a water-in-oil emulsion.[1]

Reviews describe topical dexpanthenol as acting like a moisturizer: improving stratum corneum hydration, reducing transepidermal water loss and maintaining softness and elasticity.[1] Researchers have also reported effects on fibroblast proliferation, re-epithelialization and ultraviolet-induced redness.[1] A 2020 review frames the goal of wound care as tissue that looks and functions as close to the original skin as possible, and discusses dexpanthenol among the supportive approaches.[3]

The research base consists mainly of small randomized and open-label studies on skin barrier repair, wound healing and irritation, plus registered trials in radiation dermatitis, drug-induced rashes, lip cracks and dry eye.[4][5][6][7] The first topical dexpanthenol product, Bepanthen ointment, was developed roughly 70 years before a 2017 anniversary review.[2]
infobox: Vitamin B5 analog (alcohol of pantothenic acid)
Topical (creams, ointments, eye gels, shampoos); also in parenteral B-vitamin preparations
D-form (dexpanthenol); racemic panthenol also used in cosmetics[17]

paras: In skincare, dexpanthenol appears in moisturizers, barrier creams, after-sun and post-procedure products, lip balms and baby-care ointments, usually at a few percent.[1][2] A review of common cosmeceuticals lists panthenol as one of ten ingredient groups for which clinical data on skin appearance exist, alongside vitamins A, B3, C and E, peptides, hydroxy acids, sugar amines, ceramides and metals.[8]

It is also an ingredient in some hair and scalp products. A 2020 review of telogen effluvium mentions a topical combination of caffeine, niacinamide, panthenol, dimethicone and an acrylate polymer among newer treatment options,[9] and a 24-week randomized placebo-controlled trial studied a scalp product combining antioxidants and barrier-enhancing cosmetic ingredients for hair shedding.[10] Panthenol was one component of such combinations, so the results apply to the formulations rather than to dexpanthenol alone.

Studies have tested dexpanthenol in radiation dermatitis; one randomized trial compared 0.5% dexpanthenol with 0.1% methylprednisolone in breast cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy.[4] Clinical practice guidelines on radiation reactions from the MASCC Skin Toxicity Study Group are among the literature that discusses such topical agents.[11] Registered trials have also examined it for skin rash from EGFR inhibitors, lip-corner cracks after tonsil or adenoid surgery and dry eye.[6][7][12]

A 2025 systematic review of diaper dermatitis in children, covering 13 studies and 2,935 children, reported that emollients with zinc oxide or dexpanthenol were highly effective with minimal side effects.[13] A German review of facial paresis notes that dexpanthenol eye ointment has been found useful in practice for corneal protection.[14]

Pantothenic acid is a cofactor in enzyme-catalysed reactions of carbohydrate, fatty acid and protein metabolism, and topical dexpanthenol is converted to it in tissue.[1] A randomized study of sodium lauryl sulphate-induced irritation described coenzyme A as catalysing early steps in the synthesis of fatty acids and sphingolipids, which matter for stratum corneum lipid bilayers and cell membrane integrity.[15]

The 70th-anniversary review notes that the exact mechanisms have not been fully elucidated, but molecular studies suggest dexpanthenol increases the mobility of stratum corneum components important for barrier function and modulates expression of genes involved in wound healing.[2] A randomized in vivo study of wounds reported modulation of gene expression in skin wound healing.[16]

Panthenol is a viscous, colourless, odourless liquid that dissolves readily in water and alcohol. The body rapidly oxidizes it to pantothenic acid, so it behaves as a provitamin. The D-enantiomer (dexpanthenol) is the biologically active form, and cosmetics use either D-panthenol or a racemic mixture.[17]

The first topical dexpanthenol formulation, Bepanthen ointment, was developed about seven decades before the 2017 review that marked its 70th anniversary.[2] Over that period a range of preparations tailored to individual needs has appeared, and the two main directions of use have been skin moisturizing and barrier restoration, and facilitation of wound healing.[2]

Topical dexpanthenol is generally described as well tolerated. Rare reports of skin irritation, contact dermatitis or contact allergy exist.[17] Injectable B-vitamin products that contain dexpanthenol are prescription preparations and are labelled separately.[18]

Wikipedia describes panthenol as the alcohol counterpart of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), a thick, clear, colourless liquid with the formula C9H19NO4 that dissolves easily in water and alcohol [17]. It exists in two mirror-image forms; only the D form, dexpanthenol, is biologically active, but both moisturise, so cosmetic products use either D alone or a D/L mixture [17]. Applied to skin or mucous membranes, panthenol is quickly oxidised to pantothenic acid, which is used to build coenzyme A, a cofactor in many enzymatic reactions and in cell growth [17].

Because it is water-soluble and well tolerated, dexpanthenol appears across cosmetic and pharmaceutical products: ointments and creams for dry or chapped skin, lip balms, after-sun and post-procedure care, hair and scalp products, and eye gels [1][2]. Wikipedia says it is used in pharmaceutical and children's products as a moisturiser and to speed wound healing [17]. Reviews describe the two main directions of use as skin moisturising and barrier restoration, and support of wound healing [2].

Barrier and moisturizing studies. A randomized human in vivo study examined topically applied dexpanthenol on epidermal barrier function and stratum corneum hydration.[19] A randomized trial of a dexpanthenol cream after sodium lauryl sulphate irritation reported enhanced barrier repair and reduced inflammation.[15] A controlled clinical trial of panthenol-based formulations examined skin moisturizing effects.[20] A registered phase 2 study compared the moisturizing effect of two dexpanthenol formulations in 19 people.[5]

Wound healing. A phase 4 molecular-level study examined 5% dexpanthenol ointment on superficial injuries in 15 subjects,[21] and a randomized trial reported that dexpanthenol modulated gene expression in skin wound healing.[16] A pilot study in 28 patients with wounds and a phase 3 trial of an ointment in 80 people with diabetic foot ulcers are also registered.[22][23]

Irritation and radiation reactions. The radiation dermatitis trial compared dexpanthenol with a topical corticosteroid.[4] A registered phase 3 trial of Bepanthen versus cetomacrogol in 160 people with EGFR-inhibitor rash has also been run,[6] and a phase 2 trial of a dexpanthenol mouthwash for radiation oral mucositis enrolled 30 participants.[24]

Other conditions. A randomized trial of lip-corner cracks after tonsil and adenoid surgery enrolled 106 children,[7] and two dry-eye gel trials of 24 and 125 participants have been registered.[12][25] Appearance outcomes such as skin texture or anti-aging have not been the main endpoints of most of these studies.

Dexpanthenol and vitamin B5 come up occasionally in forum threads on B-complex supplements and shampoos for athletes, such as T Nation discussions of B-complex products and shampoo choices.[26][27] These discussions are brief and mention panthenol as an ingredient or supplement component rather than as a main topic.
